lines: One became president after his boss lasted just a month.
Another took the oath beside a grieving first lady on an airplane.
And one reached the White House without ever winning a presidential or vice-presidential election.
These are all fifteen U.S. vice presidents who became president, how they got there, and what happened after the promotion.
One new president's dad even has to bring out a lamp.
It starts with John Adams, George Washington's vice president.
For eight years, Washington leaned on his cabinet while Adams complained about how insignificant his own job was.
Then Washington retired, and Adams won the election of 1796.
There was one awkward detail.
Under the original electoral system, the runner-up became vice president.
So Adams got Thomas Jefferson, the man who had just run against him.
His defeated opponent was now his deputy.
Four years later, Jefferson ran against him again.
This time Adams lost, but Jefferson still had somebody to beat.
His own running mate, Aaron Burr, had received exactly as many electoral votes.
Back then, electors didn't cast separate votes for president and vice president.
The tie went to the House of Representatives, which took thirty-six ballots to choose Jefferson.
America had almost elected the running mate instead of the intended president.
Jefferson finally took office in 1801 and later approved the Louisiana Purchase.
The Twelfth Amendment changed the electoral system afterward.
After Jefferson, another sitting vice president wouldn't win the presidency until Martin Van Buren in 1836.
Andrew Jackson's trusted ally looked like a natural successor.
Then, just months into his presidency, the Panic of 1837 hit.
Banks failed, businesses collapsed, and the country fell into a depression.
Van Buren inherited troubles that had been building before he arrived.
Voters still handed him the bill.
In 1840, they replaced him with William Henry Harrison.
Harrison's vice president was John Tyler, and Tyler's promotion came much faster.
